summary: This unit teaches you to plan and organise a small electrical team's work, day by day and week by week. You will learn to turn instructions into clear objectives, set priorities and the order of work, estimate times, share tasks by competence, prepare materials, tools and test instruments, and build safe isolation and permits into the plan. You will also learn to set out a safe work area, track progress, deal with changes, report clearly and use each week's results to plan the next one better.

blocks.p: Every morning a team leader has to answer the same questions. What are we doing today? Who is doing what, with what, and in what order? How will we stay safe? How will we know it is done? This unit is about answering them well. It is for Level 3 electricians who organise a small team on a job. The unit 'Plan a complete activity' covers a whole job from quotation to handover, with network diagrams and costing; this unit is about organising your team's work day by day and week by week.

blocks.h: What you must be able to do

head: Task
What it looks like on the job
rows: Read the job card, drawings and your supervisor's instructions, and confirm the scope, revision, deadline and the client's limits before you plan.
Turn the job into clear daily and weekly targets that anyone can check.
Set priorities and the order of work
Deal with danger first, then urgent and important work, and put tasks in an order that keeps the work flowing.
Work out how long tasks take, including set-up, isolation, testing and clear-up, with a little spare time.
Give tasks to people by competence, pair trainees with experienced electricians, delegate clearly and check the work.
Check stock, tools, test instruments, lock-off kit, PPE and access equipment before the day starts.
Build safe isolation, permits, barriers, PPE and emergency arrangements into the plan.
Set out a safe, tidy, efficient area, and leave it safe at the end of each day.
Agree times and areas with the client and other trades, and keep them informed.
Track progress against the plan, find the causes of delay and re-plan without cutting safety.
Write the daily report, warn your supervisor early, and use planned and actual times to plan better.

ul: Most sites work from about 7:00 or 7:30 a.m. to 4:00 or 4:30 p.m., with a lunch break. Occupied buildings such as schools, offices, hotels and clinics may allow noisy work or shutdowns only at set times.
Heat is a planning issue. Roof spaces under zinc and concrete roofs become dangerously hot from late morning, so plan that work early in the day.
The rainy seasons (roughly May to June and September to November) and the hurricane season (1 June to 30 November) stop outdoor work at short notice. Always have indoor work ready to switch to.

A new or altered installation must be inspected under the **Government Electrical Regulator (GER)** before JPS will connect it, and JPS sets its own dates for connections and planned outages. These are fixed points your plan must work around.
Public holidays, school terms and the client's busy times, such as the Christmas season in shops, all affect when work can be done.

blocks.note: A plan is not paperwork for its own sake. A team with a clear plan wastes less time, makes fewer mistakes and has fewer accidents, because everyone knows what they are doing and what the hazards are.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: Read the sections in order: they follow the way a team leader prepares, runs and reviews the work. Work through the examples with a calculator. Then try the practice test and read every explanation. Your instructor will show you the Centre's planning forms, task board and daily report.

sections.title: Understanding the job and setting objectives

blocks.p: Before you plan, be sure you know exactly what is wanted. Many wasted days on site start with a misunderstanding.

head: Source
What it tells you
rows: What is to be done, where, for whom, by when, and who you report to
Positions, circuits, ratings, materials and standards. Take them from the controlled set and check the revision.
The hazards and how the work is to be done safely
Where your work fits with other trades, inspections and deadlines
Working hours, areas you may use, when power can be off, security and site rules
Priorities, changes and anything that is not written down
What is finished, what is waiting and what went wrong

ul: Exactly which rooms, floors or circuits are included, and which are not
Which drawing revision to work to
The finish date, and any fixed dates inside the job: an inspection, a JPS outage, the client moving in
When and where the team can work, and when the power can be off
Who supplies the materials, and where they are
Who you report to, and who on the client's side you deal with each day

blocks.note: If a spoken instruction and the drawing disagree, or an instruction changes the work, ask your supervisor to confirm it in writing before you act. It protects the team, the client and you.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: An objective says what the team will achieve. A good one is **SMART**:

head: Letter
Meaning
Electrical example
rows: Specific: says exactly what work, and where
Second fix of lights and switches in rooms 5 to 8
Measurable: you can count or check it
16 lights and 8 switches fitted and checked working
Achievable (or agreed): possible with the people, materials and time available
Two electricians, materials on site, power-off time confirmed
Relevant: moves the job towards its goal

blocks.p: 'Get the lighting moving' is not an objective: at 4 p.m. nobody can say whether it was met. 'Rooms 5 to 8: 16 lights and 8 switches fitted and checked by 3:30 p.m.' can be checked by anyone.

blocks.note: Measure progress in **finished, checked work**: lights fitted and working, circuits tested and recorded. Hours on site and cable taken from the van do not tell you how much is done.
blocks.label: Tip

sections.title: Setting priorities and the order of work

ol: **Danger to people.** A burning smell, a damaged live cable, an exposed live part: make it safe at once by isolating, locking off and tagging, then plan the repair.
**Urgent and important.** Work with a fixed, near deadline, or a serious effect if it is late: restoring supply to a cold room or a clinic, finishing before a booked inspection.
**Important but not urgent.** Planning, training, instrument calibration, ordering long-delivery items. Give it a time in the plan, or it will become urgent.
**Urgent but less important.** Interruptions and small requests. Delegate them or fit them in.
**Neither.** Do it in spare moments, or drop it.

head: How important
Urgent
Not urgent
rows: Do now: make a hazard safe; restore a critical supply; meet a booked inspection
Plan a time: training, calibration, ordering long-lead items, next week's plan
Delegate or fit in: a client's small request, a call for information
Fill gaps or drop: tidying files, tasks nobody needs yet

blocks.p: Many electrical tasks depend on others. For each task, find what must be finished before it can start, and what is waiting for it. A typical new installation runs like this:

flow: Survey and set out
Containment and first fix
First-fix inspection, before walls and ceilings are closed
Other trades close walls and ceilings, plaster and paint
Second fix: accessories, fittings, board
Testing and the certificate
Inspection under the GER
JPS connection or reconnection
Handover to the client

ul: **Group work by area.** Finish one room or floor before moving on, so that tools, ladders, locks and materials move less.
**Do work that needs the power off** in the time the client allows: early, late, at weekends or in an agreed window. Do everything else outside that window.
**Do noisy and dusty work** when the area and its neighbours are empty.
**Order long-delivery items first** (boards, special fittings, large cables), so that they arrive before they are needed.
**Leave second fix** until plastering and painting are done, so that accessories are not damaged or painted over.
**Plan roof-space work** for the early morning, before the heat builds.

blocks.note: Before you fix the order, ask: 'What could stop this task from starting?' Materials, another trade, a permit, an inspection or a shutdown date. Deal with those first.
blocks.label: Tip

sections.title: Estimating time and building the plan

head: Part of the task
Includes
rows: Signing in, the briefing, collecting keys and permits
Barriers, access equipment, protecting floors, laying out tools and materials
Switching off, locking off, tagging and proving dead with a proven tester
Taken from your own records or the firm's figures
Your own checks, dead tests and recording the results
Removing waste, securing loose ends, restoring supplies or leaving isolations as planned
Test sheets and the daily report

blocks.p: Leaving out everything except 'the work itself' is the commonest reason plans fail. The other steps take real time on every task.

**Labour-hours** (person-hours) are the total amount of work: time per item × number of items × people needed for each item. **Duration** is how long it takes on the calendar: labour-hours ÷ the number of people who can work on it at the same time.

**Worked example 1.** 18 outlets, each taking one electrician 40 minutes: 18 × 40 = 720 minutes = 12 labour-hours. With three electricians each doing their own outlets, the duration is 12 ÷ 3 = 4 hours, plus set-up, testing and clear-up.

**Worked example 2.** 12 ceiling fans, each needing two people for 50 minutes: 12 × 50 = 600 minutes = 10 hours for the pair, which is 2 × 10 = 20 labour-hours. One pair takes 10 working hours; two pairs take about 5.
**Worked example 3.** The team starts at 7:00 a.m. The briefing takes 20 minutes, isolation and set-up 30 minutes, the work 4 hours 30 minutes, lunch 45 minutes, and testing and clear-up 45 minutes.

Add a little spare time, called **contingency** or a buffer, for small delays: a missing fixing, a wall that is harder than expected, a client's question. About 10% is common for straightforward work; allow more in old buildings, where hidden problems are likely. Contingency is not padding: if it is not needed, start the next task.

blocks.h: Where the time figures come from

ul: Records of how long tasks really took on similar jobs: the best source
The firm's standard times
The experienced electricians in your team: ask them
Adjust for the conditions: work from a tower, an occupied building, furniture in the way, old wiring, heat

head: Tool
Use it for
rows: The day's objective, tasks, people, times, materials, isolations and hazards
Task board (whiteboard or chart with columns: to do, in progress, waiting, done and checked)
Seeing at a glance who is doing what and what is finished, and updating it during the day
Tasks for each day by person or area, with fixed dates such as inspections and shutdowns marked
Your own list of tasks, deadlines, calls to make and things to order

blocks.note: Put the plan where the team can see it. A task board on the site office wall, updated at break and at lunch, does more than a perfect plan in your pocket.
blocks.label: Tip

sections.title: Sharing out the work and leading the team

ul: Each person's training, experience, and what they have been assessed as competent to do
Who is authorised for safety-critical work, such as safe isolation, terminating boards and testing
Who is still learning, and what they need to practise next
Anyone with a health problem, a limit on work at height or other restrictions

head: Task
Give it to
Why
rows: Terminating a board; testing and certification
A competent electrician, with a trainee alongside to learn
It must be right first time, and someone signs for it
It should not always fall on the newest person

ul: Share the work fairly, and give people a chance to learn something new under supervision.
Do not do every task yourself. Your job is to lead, check and keep the work flowing.
If someone says they cannot do a task safely in the time given, listen. Review the task, then change the time, the method or the help.

flow: Explain what, where and to what standard
Say how long it should take and when you will check
Point out the hazards and the controls
Make sure they have the tools, materials and drawings
Ask them to repeat the task back to you
Check at the agreed points
Give feedback; sign off only after you have checked

blocks.note: **Delegation** means giving someone a task while you stay responsible for it. You remain answerable for the quality and safety of delegated work, so check it before you report it finished.
blocks.label: Remember

ul: The day's objective, and why it matters
Each person's tasks and where they will be
Today's hazards and their controls; which circuits are isolated and who holds the locks
Permits, the times when power is off, and the client's rules
When you will check progress, and who to ask
Questions, and each person repeating back their own task

blocks.p: Keep it short (5 to 10 minutes), do it face to face at the start of the day, and record who attended. A note on the van's dashboard or a message after work is not a briefing.

blocks.h: Working with the client and other trades

ul: Get the building's programme and find out which trades will be in the same areas.
Agree with the other trades' leaders who works where and when, and the routes for cables, ducts and pipes. Involve the supervisor where needed.
Agree with the client the working hours, the rooms you may use, storage, and when power can be off, with enough notice for them to protect computers and tell their staff.
Put the agreements in writing, and check in every day. Tell everyone affected as soon as anything changes.

blocks.p: A team that arrives without a part, or with a flat battery, can waste hours. Prepare the day before.

ul: Make a list from the drawings and the day's tasks, with sizes and quantities, and add sensible spares such as fixings, connectors and glands.
Check the list against the store and the van. Order or collect anything short in time, allowing for the supplier's delivery time.
When cable comes in drums or coils, round **up** to whole drums. Example: a take-off of 180 m plus 10% waste is 198 m, so two 100 m drums are needed.
Plan one trip to the supplier for everything, rather than several: it saves time and fuel.
Check deliveries against the order and the delivery note when they arrive, and report shortages and damage the same day.
Store materials securely and dry. Copper cable is a target for theft.

blocks.h: Tools, equipment and instruments: checks the day before

head: Item
Check
rows: Complete; no cracked or damaged insulation
Undamaged; inspection label in date; batteries charged
Prove the indicator on the proving unit; leads and probes undamaged
Insulation and continuity testers (or a multifunction tester)
Calibration date not passed; leads and battery good
Lock-off devices for each type of breaker, and a personal padlock and tag for each person
Right type and height for the job; inspected and undamaged
Enough for everyone and in good condition: glasses, gloves, hearing protection, dust masks, hard hats where needed

blocks.p: If an instrument is past its calibration date, do not use it: get an in-date one for the job and send the other for calibration. Results from an out-of-date instrument cannot be relied on.
Heavy items low and secured, ladders tied, nothing loose in the cab, and the van not overloaded.

ul: Plan cable lengths to reduce offcuts, and use drums in an order that leaves useful lengths.
Sort waste on site: copper offcuts kept for recycling (they belong to the firm or the client, as agreed), cardboard and plastic bagged. Never burn waste on site.
Return unused materials to the store and record them.
Switch off site lights and chargers when they are not needed.

blocks.note: A van parked in the sun gets very hot inside. Do not leave cordless tool batteries, adhesives or test instruments in a closed van all day, and charge batteries in a cool, ventilated place.
blocks.label: Jamaica

sections.title: Planning safety and organising the work area

blocks.p: Safety is planned before the work, not added afterwards. For each task, ask what could go wrong and how the plan will stop it.

head: Hazard
Planned control
rows: Safe isolation of every circuit worked on: switch off, lock off with each worker's own lock, tag, and prove dead with a tester proved before and after. No live work.
Generators, solar PV and UPS units found and isolated
The right access equipment, inspected; towers with guard rails; nobody working alone at height
Drawings checked, a detector used, routes chosen to avoid cables and pipes
Extraction, masks and hearing protection; timing when others are away
Early starts for roof spaces, water, shade and planned breaks
Two-person lifts for drums and boards; trolleys
Barriers and signs, warning users before switching off, protecting their equipment
A first-aider, a first-aid kit, an extinguisher, the way out, and the emergency numbers: 110 for ambulance and fire, 119 for police

blocks.p: For each board or circuit, the plan states where it is isolated, who isolates it, when, who proves it dead, and when and how the supply will be restored.

head: Circuit
Isolated at
Locks
Proved dead by
Restored
rows: Kerron, with a tester proved before and after
End of day, after testing, by Kerron

blocks.p: Some clients require a **permit to work** before work in a plant room, on a main board or above a ceiling, and a **hot-work permit** for grinding or other work that makes sparks. Arrange permits while planning, not on the morning, because the client's engineer may need notice. A permit records the work, the hazards, the precautions and the times, and it is signed off when the work ends.

ul: Agree the area with the client and keep it as small as the work allows.
Put up barriers and signs to keep others out and to give the team safe room to work.
Keep exits, walkways, stairs and fire extinguishers clear. Never leave drums or conduit across a doorway or on stairs.
Have one place for tools, one for materials and one for waste, close to the work.
Protect the client's floors and furniture with sheets.
Route leads off walkways, and set steps and towers on firm, level ground.

blocks.h: At the end of every day

flow: Stop in time: plan 20 to 30 minutes for clear-up
Make safe: terminate, or insulate and cover, loose ends; fit covers to boards and boxes
Leave isolations locked and tagged, or restore the supply only after testing, as the plan says
Clear the waste and sweep up
Lock away tools and materials
Walk round and check; tell the client what is safe to use

blocks.note: Others may restore a supply or touch your work after you leave. An open board, a bare cable end or an isolation without a lock and tag, left overnight, can kill someone who does not know the work is unfinished.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.p: Watch for heavy sweating, headache, dizziness, cramps and nausea. Stop the person working, move them to shade, cool them and give them water. Confusion or collapse is an emergency: call 110.

Longer days to catch up bring tiredness, poor light and more mistakes. Before you plan them, consider whether the team will be too tired to work safely, whether there is enough light, whether the client and your supervisor agree, the security of the building, and how people will get home.

sections.title: Monitoring progress, dealing with changes and reporting

ul: Set targets in finished, checked work at the start of the day.
Check at set times, such as break, lunch and mid-afternoon: look at the work and talk to each person.
Mark progress on the task board and compare it with the plan. Example: at the halfway point of the day, about half of the day's target should be done.
Look at quality as well as quantity: work that fails inspection is not progress.

flow: Find out why: missing material, a hidden problem, a harder task, someone needing help
Choose an action: move people, change the order, get the material, get help, or reduce the target
Never skip isolation, safety steps or testing to catch up
Tell the supervisor early, with the reason and a realistic new time
Record it in the daily report

blocks.h: Common changes and what to do

head: Change
What to do
rows: Move the team to indoor tasks planned for later; protect trenches and materials
Find out when they will come; do the tasks that do not need them; check the new date against the plan
A team member is off sick
Check that the people left have the skills for each task, especially isolation and testing; pair people so nobody works beyond their competence; postpone anything that can no longer be done safely
A shutdown or JPS outage date moves
Re-plan the tasks linked to it and tell everyone affected
The client asks for extra work
Get a written instruction (a variation) through the supervisor, with the price and time agreed, before doing it
Agree a new time with them and the supervisor; move to other areas meanwhile
Find what changed, stop affected work and brief the team

blocks.note: Tell your supervisor as soon as you know the job will miss a date, and why. Bad news early can be managed; bad news on the finish date cannot.
blocks.label: Remember

head: Section
What to write
rows: By area, in finished and checked units, against the day's objective
What happened, when, how long it cost and why, as facts
Incidents, near misses, hazards found, isolations left in place
Who gave them, and whether they have been confirmed in writing

blocks.note: Write facts, not opinions. 'Kerron and Annette waited from 1:00 to 1:40 p.m. for the ceiling contractor to clear room 6' helps fix the problem; 'the ceiling men are useless' does not.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: At the end of the week, compare the planned and actual times for each task. Ask the team what helped and what got in the way. Then change a few things for next week, and update your time figures with the real ones.

**Worked example.** The team planned 30 labour-hours to fit 60 outlets (30 minutes each), and it took 36 labour-hours. 36 ÷ 60 = 0.6 hours, so each outlet really took 36 minutes. The overrun was (36 − 30) ÷ 30 × 100 = **20%**. Next time, plan about 36 minutes an outlet in similar conditions, unless the cause of the delay has been removed.

ul: Keep tasks, deadlines and calls in a notebook or phone app, not in your head.
Plan tomorrow before you leave today.
Deal with each message once: act on it, delegate it, schedule it or file it.
Keep the job file in order: drawings, permits, reports and test sheets.

blocks.p: Tick each statement only when you can do it without looking at the notes.

ul: I can collect and confirm the information I need before planning, and get changed instructions in writing.
I can write a SMART objective for a team's day or week.
I can put a list of jobs in order of priority, with danger to people first.
I can order tasks so that each is ready when the next needs it, and plan shutdowns, noisy work and roof-space work for the right times.
I can estimate task times including set-up, isolation, testing and clear-up, and add contingency.
I can work out labour-hours, durations and finishing times.
I can share tasks out by competence, delegate clearly and check delegated work.
I can give a short, clear morning briefing.
I can prepare materials, tools, test instruments, lock-off kit and PPE the day before.
I can build safe isolation, permits and emergency arrangements into a plan.
I can set out a safe, efficient work area and leave it safe at the end of the day.
I can track progress, find the cause of a delay and re-plan without cutting safety.
I can handle rain, late materials, sickness, moved shutdowns and requests for extra work.
I can write a factual daily report and warn my supervisor early.
I can compare planned and actual times and use them to plan better.

terms: Briefing (toolbox talk)
A short talk at the start of the day giving out tasks, hazards, controls and times.
Competence
Proven ability to do a task safely and to the required standard.
Contingency
Spare time (or money) built into a plan for small delays; also called a buffer.
Daily report
The team leader's written record of the day's work, problems, materials, safety and the next day's plan.
Delegation
Giving a task to someone else while staying responsible for it.
Duration
How long a task takes on the calendar: labour-hours divided by the people working on it together.
Hold point
A stage where work must stop until it has been inspected, for example before walls are closed.
Isolation plan
The part of the plan that says which circuits are isolated, where, by whom, and when they are restored.
Labour-hours
The total work in a task: hours multiplied by the number of people; also called person-hours.
Lock-off device
A device that holds a breaker or switch off so that a padlock can be fitted.
Objective
A statement of what the team will achieve; it should be specific, measurable, achievable, relevant and time-bound (SMART).
Permit to work
A signed document that records the work, hazards, precautions and times agreed before work in a controlled area.
Priority
How soon a task must be done compared with others, based on how urgent and how important it is.
Programme
The plan of when each part of a job, and each trade, will be done.
Review
Comparing what was done with what was planned, to plan better next time.
Sequence
The order in which tasks are done.
Task board
A board or chart showing each task and its status, updated during the day.
Variation
A change to the agreed work, such as extra items, agreed in writing before it is done.

c1.title: An office block at a school in Morant Bay
c1.text: Andre Thompson, a Level 3 electrician, leads a team rewiring the office block and staff room of a primary school in Morant Bay, St Thomas, during term time. Classes run in the next block from 8 a.m. to 2:30 p.m. The new sub-board must be connected into the school's main board, and the principal allows the whole school's power to be off only from 2:45 p.m. to 6 p.m. Andre's team is Marlon, an experienced electrician, and two trainees, Shanique and Dwight. His first draft of the week's objective reads 'Make good progress on the office block'.

c2.title: A Monday list in Savanna-la-Mar
c2.text: At 7 a.m. on Monday, Sasha-Gaye Reid, a team leader for a contractor in Savanna-la-Mar, Westmoreland, has this list. A supermarket reports a burning smell from the outlet behind its meat display. A guest house's second fix must be finished by Tuesday evening, because its inspection is booked for Wednesday. A quotation for a church hall rewire must reach the client by Thursday. The team's two insulation testers are due for calibration in three weeks. The van needs restocking and tidying. She has two electricians and a trainee, Kadeem.

c3.title: A hardware store extension in Port Maria
c3.text: Delroy Walters leads a team of four wiring an extension to a hardware store in Port Maria, St Mary. The job includes 30 LED high-bay lights and 18 outlets. From past jobs, one high-bay light takes a pair of electricians 45 minutes from a mobile tower, and one outlet takes one electrician 50 minutes. Each working day gives about 7 hours of productive work after the briefing, set-up and clear-up. Delroy plans one pair on the lights and the other pair on the outlets, each person in that pair fitting their own outlets.

c4.title: A wet Thursday in Bog Walk
c4.text: Nordia Campbell's team is installing outdoor lighting and a new main board at a community centre in Bog Walk, St Catherine. Thursday's plan was to dig and lay the cable trench to six light poles in the morning, then change the main board from 1 p.m. in a shutdown agreed with the centre's manager. The board change needs two competent electricians. At 7 a.m. it is raining heavily, the cable delivery has moved to Friday afternoon, and Garth, one of her two licensed electricians, has called in sick.

c5.title: Corridor lighting at a hotel in Discovery Bay
c5.text: Kevin Lewis's team of four is replacing the corridor lighting on three floors of a hotel in Discovery Bay, St Ann: 96 fittings, planned at 32 a day over three days. Guests stay in the hotel throughout. At lunchtime on day 1, halfway through the working day, the task board shows 11 fittings fitted. Two electricians lost an hour, from 8 to 9 a.m., because the access tower was locked in the hotel's store and the key holder was off duty.

questions.q: What is the main weakness of Andre's draft objective?
o: Nobody can measure whether it has been met
It is too short to go on the written plan
It does not name the people who will do the work
It does not mention the school's opening hours
questions.why: 'Good progress' cannot be counted or checked, so on Friday nobody will know whether it was achieved. A SMART objective names the work, says how it will be measured and gives a deadline, for example 'office block first fix complete and inspected by 3 p.m. Thursday'.

questions.q: When should the team cut chases and drill the block walls next to the classroom block?
o: Whenever the team reaches that wall in its order
After 2:30 p.m., when classes have finished
In short bursts during the morning break
Between 8 and 9 a.m., before the day gets hot
questions.why: Chasing and drilling block is loud and dusty. Doing it after the children leave avoids disturbing lessons and keeps the dust away from them. Quieter tasks, such as fixing boxes and pulling cables, fill the morning.

questions.q: Which task should Andre plan for the 2:45 p.m. to 6 p.m. window?
o: Connecting the sub-board into the main board
Fitting the new light fittings in the staff room
Pulling the cables into the office block conduit
Fixing the conduit runs to the office block walls
questions.why: Only the connection into the main board needs the whole school's supply off, so it goes in the window the principal allows. Conduit, cables and fittings on the new office block circuits, which are not yet connected, can be done during the day.

questions.q: Andre estimates the board connection at 2 hours 20 minutes, plus 25 minutes for isolation, proving dead and set-up, and 40 minutes for testing and restoring the supply. Starting at 2:45 p.m., will the team finish by 6 p.m.?
o: No: it would end at about 7:25 p.m.
Yes, with about 35 minutes to spare
No: it would end at about 6:10 p.m.
Yes, if the testing is left until morning
questions.why: 25 + 140 + 40 = 205 minutes, or 3 hours 25 minutes, and 2:45 p.m. plus 3 h 25 min is 6:10 p.m. Andre must re-plan, for example by preparing more before the shutdown or asking for a longer window. He must not cut the testing: the supply is restored only after the work is tested.

questions.q: Which item should Sasha-Gaye deal with first, and how?
o: The guest house, since its inspection date is fixed
The supermarket outlet: isolate and make it safe
The van, as the team cannot work without stock
The quotation, or the church may choose another firm
questions.why: A burning smell from an outlet means overheating that can start a fire, so danger to people comes first: a competent electrician isolates, locks off and tags the circuit, and the repair is then planned. The guest house is urgent and important, but it is not a danger.

questions.q: How should she deal with the testers that are due for calibration in three weeks?
o: Send them both today, before the supermarket job
Have Kadeem check them against each other instead
Leave them until the due date, since there is no rush
Book a date now, with cover for while they are away
questions.why: Calibration is important but not yet urgent. If it is not booked now, both testers may run out on the same day and the team will be unable to test. Booking ahead lets her send them one at a time or arrange a spare. Comparing one with the other is not calibration.

questions.q: Which item can Sasha-Gaye best delegate to Kadeem, with clear instructions?
o: Pricing the church hall rewire for the client
Restocking the van against the stock list
Finishing the guest house terminations alone
Making the supermarket outlet safe on his own
questions.why: Restocking against a list is a task a trainee can do well, and it frees the electricians. Isolating a faulty circuit, pricing a job and unsupervised terminations need competence and authority that Kadeem does not yet have.

questions.q: How many labour-hours will the 30 high-bay lights take?
o: 90 labour-hours
11.25 labour-hours
22.5 labour-hours
45 labour-hours
questions.why: 30 × 45 minutes = 1 350 minutes = 22.5 hours for the pair. Two people work all that time, so it is 22.5 × 2 = 45 labour-hours. Labour-hours count every person's time; the pair's duration is 22.5 hours.

questions.q: What does Delroy's plan show about the two pairs?
o: Both pairs finish on the same day, so it is balanced
Neither pair can finish this week, so re-price the job
The outlet pair is done in a day, then needs work
The lights pair finishes first, then helps the others
questions.why: Outlets: 18 × 50 = 900 minutes = 15 labour-hours, about 7.5 hours each, which is just over one day. Lights: 22.5 hours for the pair, about 3.2 days. Delroy must plan the outlet pair's next tasks, or move them onto the lights, so that nobody stands idle.

questions.q: The cable for the lights comes on 100 m drums. The take-off is 236 m, and Delroy allows 10% for waste. How many drums should he order?
o: 5 drums
2 drums
3 drums
4 drums
questions.why: 236 × 1.1 = 259.6 m. Two drums (200 m) are not enough, so order 3 drums (300 m). Always round up when ordering, and return what is left to the store.

questions.q: Nordia cannot find another competent electrician for today. What should she do about the 1 p.m. shutdown?
o: Do it with a trainee standing in for Garth
Keep the board live and change it a circuit at a time
Postpone it and agree a new date with the manager
Start it at 1 p.m. and finish it on Friday morning
questions.why: The board change was planned for two competent people, and a trainee cannot replace one. Live working is never an option, and leaving a building half-connected overnight is unsafe. Postponing and agreeing a new shutdown with the manager keeps everyone safe.

questions.q: Who must Nordia tell about today's changes, and when?
o: Nobody, unless the job runs past its finish date
Only her team, at tomorrow morning's briefing
Only the supervisor, in the end-of-week report
Her supervisor and the manager, straight away
questions.why: The supervisor needs to know at once, because the finish date and other jobs may be affected, and the manager has planned the centre's day round the shutdown. Early news lets both of them adjust; news at the end of the week is too late.

questions.q: While the team is on site, the manager asks Nordia to add two floodlights over the car park. What should she do?
o: Refuse, because extra work can never be added to a job
Get it agreed in writing, through her supervisor
Fit them, then add the cost to the final bill afterwards
Fit them today, since the team is short of outdoor work
questions.why: Extra work is a variation. It must be agreed in writing, with its price and its effect on the finish date, before it is done; otherwise the firm may not be paid, and the design and inspection may not cover it.

questions.q: How does the team's progress at lunchtime compare with the plan?
o: About 69%, ahead of the 50% planned
About 11%, far behind the plan
About 34%, behind the 50% planned
About 50%, exactly as planned
questions.why: 11 of the day's 32 fittings is about 34%, but half the working day has gone, so about 50% (16 fittings) should be done. Dividing by the whole job (11 of 96, about 11%) mixes up the day's target with the job's.

questions.q: What should Kevin do so that the tower problem does not happen again tomorrow?
o: Agree today with the hotel how the team will get the tower
Have the team use corridor chairs when the tower is locked
Note it in the daily report and hope it does not recur
Start each day an hour later, when the key holder is in
questions.why: The delay came from a gap in the arrangements, not from the team. Agreeing today where the tower is kept and who opens the store removes the cause. Standing on chairs is unsafe, and starting later loses an hour every day.

questions.q: Which entry belongs in the 'problems' part of Kevin's daily report?
o: The job is going to be late because of the hotel's store
Two electricians waited 8–9 a.m. for the tower key
There was a small delay this morning, but all is fine now
The hotel staff were slow and unhelpful all of the morning
questions.why: A report records facts: who, what, when and how long, so that the cause can be dealt with and the lost time accounted for. Opinions and vague words help nobody, and blaming the client fixes nothing.

questions.q: The 96 fittings take 3.5 days in the end. If conditions are similar, what rate should Kevin plan on for the next hotel corridor job?
o: About 27 fittings a day
About 35 fittings a day
About 24 fittings a day
32 fittings a day, as before
questions.why: 96 ÷ 3.5 = about 27 fittings a day. Planning with real rates from finished jobs makes the next plan realistic; keeping the old figure repeats the overrun, unless the cause of the delay has been removed.

questions.q: Your team must pull cables through a ceiling space under a zinc roof in July. How should you plan this work?
o: Early in the morning, with water, breaks and two people
Whenever it suits, leaving breaks to each person's choice
In the early afternoon, when the ceiling space is brightest
In one long session, to get the hot work over with quickly
questions.why: Roof spaces under zinc heat up fast from late morning, and heat stress causes illness and mistakes. Plan the work early, with water, planned breaks and nobody working alone, and watch for dizziness, headache and cramps.

questions.q: At 4 p.m., a circuit your team has disconnected at the board has bare cable ends in a corridor ceiling. Work continues tomorrow. How should it be left?
o: Breaker switched off, with a note on the board
Switched back on, so the corridor lights still work
Breaker off and the board cover left off for tomorrow
Locked off and tagged, with the ends insulated
questions.why: Someone may switch the breaker on overnight or touch the ends. A lock and tag stop the supply being restored, and insulated, covered ends protect anyone who touches them. A note can be ignored, and an open board is a hazard in itself.

questions.q: The evening before a testing day, you find that the team's only insulation tester went past its calibration date last week. What should you do?
o: Use it tomorrow, as one week over makes little difference
Use it, and write 'calibration due' on each test sheet
Ask a colleague to check it against their tester instead
Get an in-date tester, and send this one for calibration
questions.why: Results from an instrument past its calibration date cannot be relied on and may not be accepted. Borrow or hire an in-date tester so the work is not held up, and send this one for calibration.
